There's one constraint: a file can't contain the SHA of the commit that adds it, because adding the file changes that SHA. So the link has to go both ways:

## Proposed design

**1. Artifact → commits (stored in the JSON).** The artifact gets a `commits` list, filled at export time from two sources:
- **made:** commits the agent made itself, read from its `git commit` outputs (`[branch sha] subject`). This is the exact list.
- **inferred:** `git log` in the repo over the exported turns' time window, for commits the parser missed. Examples: an agent running `git commit` inside a script, or Codex Desktop committing for it.

Each entry has the full SHA, subject, time and source. An inferred commit can come from someone else working on the branch at the same time, which is why the two kinds are kept apart.

**2. Commit → artifact (in git).** The artifact gets committed with git trailers, a standard part of a commit message:
```
chore: add proof of work for <private>

Agent-Work: .agent-work/feat-<private>/<private>-reuse-761bc353-t2-5.json
Agent-Thread: 761bc353-6bba-4b29-8c98-b3da275a36a2
Agent-Commits: b9541ea, cea7953
```
- **From a commit, find its proof:** `git log --format='%h %(trailers:key=Agent-Work,valueonly)'`.
- **From a proof, find its commit:** `git log -- <file>`.
- **Tooling:** GitHub shows trailers, and other tools can read them.

**3. Tooling**
- **Commit flag:** `vp run export -- … --commit` writes the artifact and commits it with those trailers, in a separate commit so the recorded SHAs don't change. Without the flag, the CLI prints the trailer lines for the agent to paste.
- **Lookup:** `vp run export -- --which <sha>` finds the proof covering a commit. It reads the trailers first, then searches `.agent-work/**/*.json`.
- **Viewer:** a "Commits" section in the proof banner with each SHA linked to the remote (GitHub URLs are built from the recorded remote), and each `git commit` row in the tree gets a SHA chip.

One question: should `--commit` be the default for the CLI, so agents always produce the linked commit? Or opt-in, with the CLI printing trailers by default? I'd make it opt-in. A tool that commits on its own can surprise you in a repo with pre-commit hooks or a dirty working tree.

## How it would work

**1. A commit index.** toolreader finds every `git commit` the agents made across all sessions (t3 and Codex). Each one becomes an anchor: SHA, repo, branch, thread, and position in that thread's timeline. Short SHAs from outputs (`cea7953`) are resolved to full ones with `git rev-parse` in that repo, when the repo still exists locally.

**2. A commit-range view: "history between A and B".**
- `git log A..B` in the repo gives the commits in the range.
- For each commit, toolreader takes the work that produced it: that thread's actions after its previous commit (or the start of that turn) up to and including this commit.
- Those segments are stitched together in commit order. Each one gets a header with the commit's SHA, subject and branch, followed by the usual phases and actions. The swimlane spans the whole range.
- If two sessions worked on the range, you see both, each under the commits it made.
- **How you open it:** with `#/commits?repo=…&from=A&to=B` in the browser, or by clicking two commit markers in a thread. Commit markers appear on the `git commit` rows and as ticks on the swimlane.

**3. Export uses the same scope.**
- `vp run export -- --repo . --commits main..HEAD` writes one artifact covering exactly the work behind a PR's commits, from however many sessions.
- Its `commits` list records which SHAs each segment belongs to.
- The trailer idea from my last message still applies to the commit that adds the file.

**What it can't map:**
- **Rewritten history.** After a rebase, `--amend` or a GitHub squash merge, the final SHAs differ from the ones the agent printed. I'd match those back by commit message plus time window and mark the match as approximate, not drop them silently.
- **Commits made by you.** Commits made outside an agent session have no history; the view shows them as "no agent history".

This maps well to git itself — a separate ref like a notes namespace or an orphan branch keyed by commit SHA could serve as that append-only ledger mirroring the commit tree.

But git notes don't survive rebases cleanly without extra config, and GitHub doesn't render them anymore, so an orphan `agent-ledger` branch with per-commit JSON files seems more durable and visible, letting a range query just walk the commits and look up each entry from the ledger offline.

The post-commit hook staying optional is a nice touch too. Now I should structure my answer: confirm it's possible, explain the mechanism, compare the two storage approaches, give my recommendation, and ask for approval before proceeding — keeping it concise.

Yes, that works, and git already has the shape for it: a separate ref whose contents are keyed by commit SHA, alongside the normal branches and never mixed into them. Your code history stays clean, and the ledger reads like an index: "commit `cea7953` → the agent work that produced it".

## How the ledger would work

**One entry per commit.** Each code commit an agent made gets one ledger entry. It holds the slice of session history that produced that commit, from the agent's previous commit (or the start of the turn) up to this one, plus:
- the thread id, the provider and the turns covered;
- outputs, redacted the same way as the proof files;
- the commit's **patch-id**, git's fingerprint of the change itself. It stays the same across rebases and amends that keep the diff, so entries can be found again after SHAs change.

**History between two commits.** `git rev-list A..B` gives the commits, each SHA looks up its entry, and the slices are shown in order in the existing viewer. This works from the repo alone: no t3 database and no Codex needed. Clone the repo, fetch the ledger, and the history is there.

**How entries get written:** `vp run ledger -- sync --repo .`.
- It finds the agent commits on the current branch (using the commit index from my last message) and writes entries for any that have none yet.
- **Running it:** by hand, by the agent before it pushes, or from an optional `post-commit` hook.
- **Safety:** it writes with git plumbing (`hash-object` / `commit-tree`), so it never checks anything out or touches your working tree.

## Where to keep it: two options

| | **A. Ledger branch** (`agent-ledger`, unrelated to the code branches) | **B. Git notes** (`refs/notes/agent-work`) |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | `commits/<sha>.json` + `patch-ids.json` index | git stores one note per commit SHA itself |
| Push / fetch | normal `git push origin agent-ledger` | needs explicit refspecs; not fetched by default |
| Visible on GitHub | yes, browsable like any branch | no (GitHub stopped showing notes) |
| After rebase / amend | found again by patch-id | git can copy notes automatically (`notes.rewriteRef`) |
| After squash merge | squashed commit has a new diff: matched by PR / branch name, marked approximate | same problem, and no lookup by patch-id |

I recommend **A, the ledger branch**: it's visible, pushes like anything else, needs no special git config, and patch-id lookup covers rebases. For squash merges, the entries stay keyed to the PR's original commits, so the squashed commit links back through its PR.

**The viewer:**
- a repo-level page that lists ledger commits along the branch;
- picking two commits shows the history between them;
- ledger entries open read-only, like proof files.
